opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot. Working on vLLM was a great experience. The core idea there, PagedAttention, was about managing KV cache memory efficiently so you could serve many requests at once with high throughput. That solved a real bottleneck, and I learned a lot about where the inefficiencies in LLM serving actually are.

But as we kept working, we noticed that the way people were *using* language models was changing. It wasn't just one prompt in, one completion out anymore. People were building agents, multi-turn chats, few-shot pipelines, tree-of-thought search, structured outputs like JSON. These are really programs that call the model many times, and the calls share a lot of structure: the same system prompt, the same few-shot examples, the same conversation prefix branching into different continuations.

Existing serving systems, vLLM included at the time, mostly treated each request independently. So you'd recompute the same prefix again and again and throw away work you'd already done. And on the frontend side, developers were writing these complex workflows with a lot of glue code and string manipulation, with no way to tell the runtime what the structure of the program was.

So the motivation for SGLang was to co-design both sides. On the frontend, a small language embedded in Python that lets you express these LLM programs naturally, with generation calls, forks, constraints, and so on. On the backend, a runtime that can exploit that structure. The best-known piece is RadixAttention, where we keep the KV cache in a radix tree so that any shared prefix across requests gets reused automatically instead of recomputed. We also did things like compressed finite-state machines for constrained decoding, so generating valid JSON is much faster.

So it wasn't that vLLM was wrong. It was more that we saw a new class of workloads emerging and felt the right answer needed a fresh design that thought about the program and the runtime together. Starting a new project gave us the freedom to rethink the architecture from that angle. And honestly, the two projects have pushed each other forward, which I think has been really good for the whole open-source inference community.

r002.rationale: It describes SGLang’s frontend, runtime, and RadixAttention, but does not say it developed from a particular innovation into a general serving engine.

r003.rationale: Calling SGLang a “new project” with a “fresh design” rejects the idea that it began as an engine inside vLLM and was later renamed or spun out.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So vLLM and SGLang actually came out of the same group at Berkeley, and the motivations were different.

vLLM was really about the engine. The question there was, how do we serve a single model as efficiently as possible? PagedAttention, memory management, batching, that kind of thing. It solved a very specific and important problem, which was that GPU memory was being wasted and throughput was much lower than it could be.

But as people started building actual applications on top of LLMs, we noticed that the workload wasn't just "send one prompt, get one answer." People were writing agents, multi-turn conversations, few-shot prompting with long shared prefixes, tree search, structured outputs with JSON constraints. These programs call the model many times, and the calls share a lot of structure. The existing serving stack treated every request as independent, so a lot of that structure was thrown away.

So SGLang started from the other side. Instead of asking how to make one forward pass fast, we asked what the programming interface should look like when you're orchestrating many LLM calls, and then what runtime you'd need to make those programs fast. That led to two pieces. One is the frontend language, which lets you express things like branching and parallel generation and constrained decoding naturally. The other is the runtime, with RadixAttention, which keeps the KV cache in a tree so that any shared prefix across requests gets reused automatically. You don't have to think about it as a user.

To be honest, I didn't think of it as leaving vLLM behind. It was more that I'd seen the engine-level problems up close, and I could see the next bottleneck was going to be at the application level. Those are two different layers, and I wanted to work on the one that nobody had really tackled yet.

astra-6.text:
For me, SGLang was a continuation of the same question: how do we make large language models more efficient to use? With vLLM, we focused on serving models efficiently, especially managing the memory used by the KV cache. But there are also opportunities at the application level that a serving engine alone doesn’t necessarily capture.

An LLM application may make several related calls, reuse the same context, or branch into multiple generations. If we treat every call as an independent request, we miss opportunities to share computation. So the motivation for SGLang was to bring the programming interface and the runtime closer together: let developers express those workflows, and let the runtime use that structure to execute them efficiently.

So it wasn’t simply about building another vLLM. It was about exploring a broader layer of optimization, across both the application and the inference engine.

sol-6.1.text:
Working on vLLM taught me a lot about making inference efficient. But I also saw that an LLM application often involves much more than a single generation call. You might have multiple calls, branching logic, structured outputs, or different requests sharing the same prompt prefix. I wanted to explore how we could optimize that whole workflow.

That was the motivation for SGLang: co-designing the programming interface and the runtime. If the system understands how an application uses the model, it has more opportunities to reuse computation and schedule work efficiently. For example, RadixAttention lets us reuse KV caches across calls that share prefixes.

So it wasn’t simply about building another inference engine. It was about exploring a broader question: how do we make complex language-model programs both easy to express and efficient to execute?
